name: Pairs inside a budget
brief:
A desk may buy two different lots from an offer list, as long as the two prices add up to at most `budget`. `prices` is sorted from cheapest to dearest, in whole pence.

Write `count_pairs_within(prices, budget)`, which counts the pairs of positions `i < j` with `prices[i] + prices[j] <= budget`. Equal prices at different positions count as different lots.

Example. For `prices = [1, 3, 4, 6, 9]` and `budget = 7` the pairs are 1 with 3, 1 with 4, 1 with 6 and 3 with 4. So the answer is 4.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ prices, sorted, each a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Checking every pair is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser. Answers can pass $10^{10}$.
hint: Start one pointer at the cheapest price and one at the dearest. If the two fit the budget, the cheap one fits with everything between them as well.

examples.note: 1 fits with 3, 4 and 6, and 3 fits with 4. That is four pairs.
Each of the three pairs costs exactly 10, which is allowed.

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: With the ends at `lo` and `hi`, a pair that fits means `lo` fits with all `hi - lo` prices up to `hi`.
The trap is moving the wrong pointer: when the pair is over budget, only dropping the dearest can help.
Each step moves one pointer inward, so the work is $O(n)$.
